1. [MATH: f] is a surjection
2. [MATH: f] is an injection
3. [MATH: f] is a bijection

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that a function [MATH: f: X \to Y] is

  • a surjection if [MATH: \forall\, y \in Y,] [MATH: \exists\, x \in X] such that [MATH: f(x)=y,]

  • an injection if [MATH: \forall\, x_1,x_2 \in X,] whenever [MATH: f(x_1)=f(x_2),] we have [MATH: x_1=x_2,]

  • a bijection if it is both a surjection and an injection.

With that in mind, let's consider each statement in turn.

  • Statement I is true. According to the diagram, for every element [MATH: y \in Y,] we have an arrow from some element [MATH: x \in X] to it, which means that [MATH: f(x)=y.] So, [MATH: f] is a surjection.

  • Statement II is false. We have [MATH: f(4)=f(6)] but [MATH: 4 \neq 6.] So, it's not true that for all [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2] contained within the domain [MATH: X,] if [MATH: f(x_1)] and [MATH: f(x_2)] are equal, then we must have [MATH: x_1=x_2.] As a result, [MATH: f] is not an injection.

  • Statement III is false. Since statement II is false, [MATH: f] is not a bijection.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

  • II is not a bijection because it is not surjective. Remember that the range of [MATH: \sin x] is [MATH: [-1,1].] This means that [MATH: -1 \leq \sin x \leq 1.] So, for example, there is no value [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}] such that [MATH: g(x) = 2.]

  • III is a bijection. First of all, [MATH: h] is a surjection because [MATH: \forall\, y \in (0, \infty),] we can choose an [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}] such that [MATH: h(x)=y\mathbin{:}] [MATH: h(x)|= y; 3^{x}|= y; \log_{3} (3^{x})|= \log_{3} (y); x|= \log_{3} (y)] Let's verify the above formula: [MATH: h(x) = h \left(\log_3\left(y\right) \right) = 3^{\log_3\left(y\right)} = y] Second, [MATH: h] is an injection: [MATH: h(x_{1})|= h(x_{2}); 3^{x_{1}}|= 3^{x_{2}}; \log_{3} (3^{x_{1}})|= \log_{3} (3^{x_{2}}); x_{1}|= x_{2}] Because [MATH: h] is both surjective and injective, we conclude that [MATH: h] is bijective.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A function [MATH: f: X \to Y] is a bijection if it is both a surjection and an injection. Recall the following:

Content:
- [MATH: f] is a surjection if [MATH: \forall\, y \in Y,] [MATH: \exists\, x \in X] such that [MATH: f(x)=y.]
- [MATH: f] is an injection if [MATH: \forall\, x_1,x_2 \in X,] whenever [MATH: f(x_1)=f(x_2),] we have [MATH: x_1=x_2.]

Content:
For example, this is an example of a bijection.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2d4bff0ab1b1c926ce29af009d19b42f]

Content:
Intuitively, a function is a bijection if

Content:
- the outputs of the function cover the entire range, and
- every output comes from a unique input (no two inputs map to the same output).

Content:
Note: A bijection is sometimes called a one-to-one correspondence because every element of the domain corresponds to exactly one element of the range, and vice versa.
